screens.title: HTTP, REST APIs, and Web Scraping for IoT
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how your IoT devices communicate with cloud services using the web's foundational protocol, HTTP, and how to both consume and build REST APIs for device data and control. We'll look at concrete Python examples that send sensor readings, parse JSON responses from public APIs like weather services, and implement small Flask endpoints to receive data and forward commands. You'll also see when web scraping is necessary, why it is fragile, and how to protect secrets with environment variables. These skills let an IoT device upload readings, fetch configuration or weather data, and accept remote control commands from a client. A short example to keep in mind: a Raspberry Pi posts temperature readings to a cloud endpoint, while a remote app sends a control command that the Pi forwards to an Arduino. By the end of the lesson you'll understand the HTTP methods commonly used in IoT, how to use the Python requests library safely, and how to structure a minimal Flask A P I that stores readings and forwards commands. Notice practical pitfalls such as leaking A P I keys and why you should prefer official APIs over scraping. Ready to explore the topics that will make your devices web-enabled and secure?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › HTTP, REST APIs, Web Scraping
HTTP, REST APIs, and Web Scraping for IoT
Make your devices send, receive, and respond to data on the web — safely and reliably.
What you'll do
Send sensor data with HTTP, consume public APIs, parse JSON, and build a Flask API to receive readings and forward commands.
Why it matters
These patterns let devices report telemetry, adapt to external data, and accept remote control, which is central to most IoT systems.
Explore Key Topics
HTTP Methods
GET, POST, PUT, DELETE for fetching, sending, updating, and removing resources.
Requests in Python
Use the requests library to call APIs and parse JSON responses easily.
Flask Endpoints
Build lightweight REST endpoints to accept sensor data and send control commands.
Coming up: practical examples that show code running on a device and a Flask server receiving and storing readings.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Device: Python client
import requests
response = requests.get("https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London&appid=YOUR_API_KEY&units=metric")
weather = response.json()
temperature = weather["main"]["temp"]
print(f"Current temperature in London: {temperature}°C")
Server: Flask receiver
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/readings', methods=['POST'])
def add_reading():
  data = request.get_json()
  # save to DB
  return jsonify({"status": "success"}), 201
Security note
Never store API keys in source. Use environment variables or protected config files on the device to keep secrets out of version control.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide your hands-on practice and assessments. First, you will learn to use Python's requests library to perform HTTP GET and POST calls to web services. Practically, that means your device can fetch weather or configuration and push sensor readings. Second, you'll consume public APIs such as weather, geolocation, or time endpoints and parse JSON to extract meaningful fields. This skill lets your device adapt to outside data, like adjusting fans based on a weather forecast. Third, you'll parse JSON responses reliably, handling missing keys and converting values for storage or display. That includes reading nested objects and lists, verifying types, and using safe access patterns so your code doesn't crash. Fourth, you'll build a REST A P I with Flask capable of receiving readings, returning historical data, and accepting control commands to forward to hardware. You will test that A P I using curl from another computer on the network. Each objective pairs a practical command or code snippet with a competency check so you can verify your system sends, stores, and responds to data securely. These objectives keep the focus on reliable data flow and safe secret handling.

screens.title: HTTP methods in IoT
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP provides a small set of standard methods that map naturally to IoT tasks. GET retrieves data: use it when a device or client needs to fetch configuration, the latest readings, or external data like weather. POST sends new data: use it when your device uploads a telemetry record or a log entry. PUT updates an existing resource, for example changing a device's saved configuration; it generally replaces or updates the target resource. DELETE removes a resource, such as unregistering a device or deleting old stored entries. A concrete example: a device posts a sensor reading with POST to the readings endpoint, a dashboard fetches recent readings with GET, an operator updates reporting settings with PUT, and a cleanup job deletes obsolete records with DELETE. A common misconception is thinking POST and PUT are identical. They are different in intent: POST creates or appends, while PUT is intended for an idempotent update. For IoT, that distinction matters when retries happen on poor networks — a repeated POST can create duplicate records while a properly designed PUT should not. As a takeaway, map your device operations to the right method, design endpoints to be safe on retry, and document expected behavior for clients.

keyIdea.title: HTTP methods
keyIdea.text: Map IoT actions to GET for read, POST for create/send, PUT for update, and DELETE for removal; design endpoints with retry behaviors in mind.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › HTTP methods in IoT
HTTP methods explained
Definitions, concrete device examples, and a retry misconception.
GET — read
Fetch configuration or recent readings. Safe and typically cacheable.
POST — create/send
Upload sensor telemetry or logs. May create new records on each call.
PUT — update
Update an existing resource, such as device configuration. Expect idempotent behavior when designed correctly.
DELETE — remove
Remove resources like old readings or deregister a device.
Key Takeaway

Choose methods intentionally: GET for safe read, POST for new submissions, PUT for controlled updates, and DELETE for removals. Design with retries in mind.

Concrete scenario
A Raspberry Pi periodically POSTS temperature readings to a cloud endpoint. A mobile dashboard GETs the latest readings to display trends. An admin uses PUT to change the device's reporting interval. A cleanup job issues DELETE to remove data older than a retention window.
Common misconception
People sometimes use POST for updates because it 'works'. That causes duplicate records when clients retry. Prefer PUT for idempotent updates or design your POST to detect duplicates.
Check your understanding
  • When should a device use GET vs POST?
  • Why does idempotence matter on flaky networks?
  • How would you prevent duplicate readings on retries?

screens.title: Using Python's requests library
screens.narratorSegment: The requests library is the go-to tool in Python for simple HTTP operations from devices. A GET request fetches a resource and returns a response object you can convert to JSON. For example, calling a public weather endpoint returns a JSON object where temperature typically sits under a main object and a temp key. You call response. json() to parse that payload into Python dictionaries and lists. A POST request sends data to a server. The chapter shows a POST that sends sensor fields using a payload dictionary to a Thingspeak-like update endpoint. Note the difference between sending form-encoded data with a data parameter and sending JSON with a json parameter; many APIs expect one or the other. A common error is printing or assuming keys exist in the JSON without checking; use methods that handle missing entries gracefully. Also never hardcode A P I keys—use environment variables and read them with os. environ. get. Practically, test both GET and POST from your device, watch response. status_code to confirm success, and print response text on failures to debug. Try the example GET for weather and the POST that uploads two fields to verify round-trip behavior before wiring these calls into your main device loop.

keyIdea.title: requests basics
keyIdea.text: Use requests.get to fetch JSON and requests.post to send data; parse with response.json() and check response.status_code. Avoid hardcoding keys.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Python requests
GET example (weather)
Fetch current temperature and parse JSON safely.
import requests

response = requests.get("https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London&appid=YOUR_API_KEY&units=metric")
if response.status_code == 200:
  weather = response.json()
  temperature = weather.get("main", {}).get("temp")
  print(f"Current temperature in London: {temperature}°C")
else:
  print("Failed to fetch weather", response.status_code)
Use dict.get to avoid KeyError if fields are missing. Check status_code before parsing.
POST example (sensor upload)
Send sensor fields to a cloud update endpoint and examine the response status.
import requests

payload = {
  "api_key": "YOUR_KEY",
  "field1": 25.5,
  "field2": 60.0
}
response = requests.post("https://api.thingspeak.com/update", data=payload)
print(f"Response status: {response.status_code}")
Some APIs require form data and others expect JSON. Read the API docs and use data= or json= accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Use response.status_code to detect success and response.json() to get structured data. Never assume keys exist.

screens.title: Parsing JSON responses for device logic
screens.narratorSegment: JSON is the most common payload format when calling web APIs. When your device receives JSON, it becomes a nested set of dictionaries and lists in Python after calling response. json(). The practical steps are: parse the JSON, check for expected keys, convert the extracted values to the needed type, and handle missing or malformed values. For example, the weather JSON usually nests main. temp under main, so access that path using safe access like dict. get and default fallbacks. Always validate the type — a numeric string may need conversion to float before storage. A concrete example: request weather, then obtain temperature with weather. get('main', {}). get('temp'). If the value is None, decide whether to retry or use a cached reading. A common misconception is trusting that the A P I always returns full data; networks and services fail, so include error handling and retry policies. Also consider that parsing large JSON structures on small devices uses memory; extract only relevant fields and avoid holding entire payloads when unnecessary. As a takeaway, treat JSON as structured data that must be validated and sanitized before being used by device logic or inserted into a database.

keyIdea.title: JSON parsing
keyIdea.text: Use response.json(), access nested fields with safe patterns, validate types, and handle missing values and retries to make device logic robust.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Parsing JSON
Safe JSON access pattern
Use nested gets and validate values before use.
# parse and extract safely
weather = response.json()
temp = weather.get('main', {}).get('temp')
if temp is None:
  # handle missing value: retry or use fallback
  pass
else:
  temp_value = float(temp)
  # store or act on temp_value
Check for None, convert types explicitly, and avoid indexing into nested structures without safeguards to prevent runtime errors on devices.
Memory and performance
Small devices have limited RAM. Only keep necessary fields and process streams incrementally if payloads are large.
Example: converting types
If a numeric value arrives as text, convert it before storing in SQLite to ensure correct column types and comparisons.
Key Takeaway

Treat JSON as untrusted input: validate structure and types, handle missing values, and minimize memory use on devices.

screens.title: Consume public APIs from your IoT device
screens.narratorSegment: When consuming public APIs from an IoT device, follow a clear process that keeps reliability and security in mind. Step one: read the A P I documentation to learn required parameters and authentication. For example, many weather services require an A P I key and specific query parameters for city and units. Step two: implement a lightweight request using the requests library, check response. status_code, and parse response. json() to extract the fields you need. Step three: validate and transform values for your device logic, for instance converting a temperature to a float or mapping a string status to a numeric threshold. Step four: handle errors and network issues with retry logic, exponential backoff, and caching where appropriate so your device can continue operating if the external A P I is temporarily unreachable. Step five: secure A P I keys by storing them in environment variables and not in source control. A concrete example is fetching the current temperature and adjusting a fan speed based on a threshold. A common misconception is polling too frequently; public APIs often have rate limits. Design your device to poll only as often as necessary and cache results when possible. The result is a predictable, secure integration between device logic and external data sources.

keyIdea.title: Consume APIs safely
keyIdea.text: Follow API docs, check responses, validate data, implement retries and caching, and secure keys to integrate external data into device logic responsibly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Consume public APIs
1. Read the docs & get a key
Identify required parameters, authentication method, and rate limits before coding.
2. Request and verify
Call the endpoint, check response.status_code, and parse JSON only on success.
3. Validate & convert
Convert types and guard against missing fields before acting on values.
4. Retry, cache, respect rate limits
Implement retries and caching to avoid hitting rate limits and handle transient failures.
Concrete example
Fetch temperature, parse float, then adjust fan speed threshold. Cache the last successful value for 5 minutes to avoid excess polling.
Polling pitfall
Polling too frequently can exhaust API quotas. Respect documented limits and use sensible defaults for embedded devices.
Key Takeaway

Consume APIs thoughtfully: follow docs, protect keys, validate data, and avoid excessive polling to keep integrations reliable.

screens.title: REST API design for IoT gateways
screens.narratorSegment: REST APIs for IoT typically expose resources such as devices and readings through clear, resource-based URLs. The chapter lists common endpoints like GET /api/devices to list registered devices, GET /api/devices/001/readings to fetch recent readings, POST /api/devices/001/readings to upload a new reading, PUT /api/devices/001/config to update settings, and DELETE /api/devices/001 to remove a device. Two important architectural principles are stateless communication and clear resource modeling. Stateless means each request contains all information required to process it; the server does not rely on stored session state from previous calls. For IoT, stateless APIs simplify scaling, retries, and failure recovery. Resource-based URLs make intent explicit: an endpoint name indicates the object being manipulated. When designing such APIs, think about the data model for readings, how many results to return by default, and how to document expected payload shapes. A common misconception is coupling device transport state to the A P I; instead, design the A P I to accept well-formed JSON payloads and let the server handle persistence. As a takeaway, model devices and readings as resources, keep endpoints stateless, and document expected request and response formats for clients.

keyIdea.text: Model devices and readings as resources with stateless endpoints so clients can retry and servers can scale without session dependence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › REST API design
Common endpoints
  • GET /api/devices — list registered devices.
  • GET /api/devices/{id}/readings — get recent readings for a device.
  • POST /api/devices/{id}/readings — upload a new reading.
  • PUT /api/devices/{id}/config — update device configuration.
  • DELETE /api/devices/{id} — remove a device.
Document the expected JSON body for each endpoint and the response codes clients should expect. That clarity reduces integration errors.
Statelessness explained
Each API request should carry required data so the server does not depend on previous interactions. This simplifies retries and horizontal scaling.
Design question
If a POST is retried, how will your server detect duplicates? Consider unique client-side identifiers or short-term deduplication logic.
Key Takeaway

Model endpoints around resources, keep calls stateless, and document request/response shapes to enable robust client-server interactions.

screens.title: Build a Flask REST API to receive readings
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter supplies a compact Flask example that demonstrates the core endpoints an IoT gateway needs. The server exposes a POST endpoint to receive readings, a GET endpoint to query recent readings, and a POST control endpoint that can forward commands to attached hardware. In the provided code, the POST reading handler calls request. get_json() to parse the incoming JSON, extracts timestamp, sensor_id, and value, writes them into a local SQLite database, and returns a JSON success response with a 201 status code. The GET endpoint queries the database for the last ten rows for a sensor and returns them as JSON. A practical lab step is to test the POST using curl from another computer, ensuring the server returns 201 and the data appears in SQLite. Another detail: the control endpoint reads a command from JSON and can forward it to an Arduino via serial — the code comments show where to integrate serial forwarding. A common misconception is exposing control endpoints without authentication; in a real deployment add authentication and validation before forwarding commands. As a takeaway, this minimal Flask pattern is enough to accept telemetry and control commands in many IoT setups, and testing with curl confirms end-to-end behavior.

keyIdea.title: Flask for IoT
keyIdea.text: A small Flask app can accept JSON readings, store them in SQLite, return recent data, and forward commands to hardware with careful validation and testing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Flask REST API
Server code (excerpt)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import sqlite3

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/readings', methods=['POST'])
def add_reading():
    data = request.get_json()
    timestamp = data.get('timestamp')
    sensor_id = data.get('sensor_id')
    value = data.get('value')

    conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("INSERT INTO sensor_readings VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
              (timestamp, sensor_id, value))
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()
    return jsonify({"status": "success"}), 201
This handler parses JSON, inserts into SQLite, and returns 201 on success. Validate fields before inserting in production.
GET and control endpoints
@app.route('/api/readings/<sensor_id>', methods=['GET'])
def get_readings(sensor_id):
    conn = sqlite3.connect('iot_data.db')
    c = conn.cursor()
    c.execute("SELECT * FROM sensor_readings WHERE sensor_id = ? ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10",
              (sensor_id,))
    rows = c.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return jsonify(rows)

@app.route('/api/control', methods=['POST'])
def control_device():
    data = request.get_json()
    command = data.get('command')
    # Forward command to Arduino via serial

screens.title: Forwarding control commands to hardware
screens.narratorSegment: A control endpoint lets remote users or apps send commands to a connected device. In the chapter's Flask example, the control handler reads a command from JSON and includes a commented line showing where to write that command to a serial connection to an Arduino. The core idea is simple: validate the incoming command, then forward it over a reliable transport to the microcontroller. In practice, avoid blocking serial writes on the main request thread. Instead, queue commands for a background worker or use a non-blocking serial write so the A P I remains responsive. A concrete scenario: a POST to /api/control carries a command like 'LED_ON'; the Flask server validates the command against a whitelist, then sends it over serial to the Arduino which executes the action. A common misconception is treating remote control endpoints as inherently safe; always authenticate and validate commands and consider rate limiting to avoid abuse. For testing, post a command and watch the hardware respond, but plan to add authentication and logging in production. The key is to separate network-facing logic from hardware input and output so network failures do not block or corrupt device control flows.

Command flow
Validate, queue, and forward commands to hardware safely.
Validate commands
Whitelist allowed commands and sanitize inputs before forwarding to hardware.
Non-blocking I/O
Use a background worker or non-blocking writes so the server stays responsive under load.
Logging & auth
Log commands for audit and secure the endpoint so only authorized clients can control hardware.
Concrete scenario
A mobile app posts a command to turn an LED on. The server checks that 'LED_ON' is allowed, places it on a queue, and a background thread writes to serial for the Arduino to act on.

Forwarding unvalidated input directly to hardware can produce unsafe behavior or allow injection-style faults.

Keep network-facing control logic separate from hardware I/O, validate commands, and process hardware writes in the background for reliability.

screens.title: Web scraping with BeautifulSoup
screens.narratorSegment: Web scraping extracts data from H T M L when no A P I exists, but it should be a last resort. The chapter shows a simple BeautifulSoup example that requests a web page and searches for a span element with a temperature class to extract its text. This approach works quickly, but it is fragile: websites change markup, class names, or structure without notice. Additionally, scraping can conflict with a site's terms of service. If you must scrape, minimize risk by writing resilient selectors, handling missing elements gracefully, and caching results. The provided code pattern is: request the page, parse response. text with BeautifulSoup, find the target element, and extract its text. A concrete example is locating a span with class 'temperature' and printing its content. A common misconception is that scraping is just as reliable as an A P I; it is not. When scraping, include error handling for when elements are not found and consider politeness measures like reduced frequency and respect for robots directives. As a takeaway, use BeautifulSoup only if there's no A P I, and treat scraped data as volatile and untrusted.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Web Scraping
BeautifulSoup example
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import requests

response = requests.get("https://example.com/weather")
soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, 'html.parser')
temp = soup.find('span', class_='temperature').text
print(f"Scraped temperature: {temp}")
This extracts a span with a specific class. If the page structure changes, the find call may return None, so add checks.
When to prefer APIs
APIs provide structured, stable data designed for consumption. Use scraping only if no API exists and the site permits it.
Fragility warning
Web markup changes can silently break scrapers. Add monitoring and fallbacks when relying on scraped data.

Scraping works but is brittle and may violate terms. Prefer APIs, and if scraping is necessary, build resilient selectors and caching.

screens.title: API keys and environment variables
screens.narratorSegment: Protecting A P I keys and credentials is a critical part of building IoT systems. The chapter shows reading keys from environment variables with os. environ. get and setting them on the Raspberry Pi using export in a shell or systemd configuration. Hardcoding keys in source code is risky because code is often shared, pushed to repositories, or inspected during debugging. A better approach is to place keys in environment variables and reference them at runtime. On a Raspberry Pi, you can set export THINGSPEAK_API_KEY in a profile or configure the systemd service environment. For example, in Python use API_KEY = os. environ. get('THINGSPEAK_API_KEY') so the running process reads the secret from the environment. A common misconception is that environment variables are magically secure; they are better than source code, but you still must restrict who can read system files and avoid printing secrets in logs. Also consider file permissions and private configuration stores for more stringent deployments. As a takeaway, never place secrets in code that may be committed. Use environment variables or a protected config and audit access to those secrets to reduce the risk of leakage.

Storing API keys

import os
API_KEY = os.environ.get('THINGSPEAK_API_KEY')

Hardcode
Easy but unsafe. Keys may be exposed via commits, shared archives, or logs.
Environment
Safer and standard for deployment. Still protect access to the environment and avoid printing secrets.

Use environment variables for API keys, secure access to system files, and never print secrets in logs or error messages.

In this chapter you will learn how your IoT devices communicate with cloud services using the web's foundational protocol, HTTP, and how to both consume and build REST APIs for device data and control. We'll look at concrete Python examples that send sensor readings, parse JSON responses from public APIs like weather services, and implement small Flask endpoints to receive data and forward commands. You'll also see when web scraping is necessary, why it is fragile, and how to protect secrets with environment variables. These skills let an IoT device upload readings, fetch configuration or weather data, and accept remote control commands from a client. A short example to keep in mind: a Raspberry Pi posts temperature readings to a cloud endpoint, while a remote app sends a control command that the Pi forwards to an Arduino. By the end of the lesson you'll understand the HTTP methods commonly used in IoT, how to use the Python requests library safely, and how to structure a minimal Flask A P I that stores readings and forwards commands. Notice practical pitfalls such as leaking A P I keys and why you should prefer official APIs over scraping. Ready to explore the topics that will make your devices web-enabled and secure?

These objectives guide your hands-on practice and assessments. First, you will learn to use Python's requests library to perform HTTP GET and POST calls to web services. Practically, that means your device can fetch weather or configuration and push sensor readings. Second, you'll consume public APIs such as weather, geolocation, or time endpoints and parse JSON to extract meaningful fields. This skill lets your device adapt to outside data, like adjusting fans based on a weather forecast. Third, you'll parse JSON responses reliably, handling missing keys and converting values for storage or display. That includes reading nested objects and lists, verifying types, and using safe access patterns so your code doesn't crash. Fourth, you'll build a REST A P I with Flask capable of receiving readings, returning historical data, and accepting control commands to forward to hardware. You will test that A P I using curl from another computer on the network. Each objective pairs a practical command or code snippet with a competency check so you can verify your system sends, stores, and responds to data securely. These objectives keep the focus on reliable data flow and safe secret handling.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and cautious choices. You will implement Flask endpoints to receive sensor data and to accept control commands, then test them with curl from another machine. Testing ensures your device can both store readings into a local SQLite database and forward commands to attached hardware. You will also practice web scraping with BeautifulSoup as a fallback when no A P I exists, and you will learn the limitations: scraping is brittle because websites change and might violate terms. In the lab you will exercise a three-endpoint A P I: a POST endpoint to receive sensor readings and store them, a GET endpoint to retrieve the last ten readings for a sensor, and a POST control endpoint that forwards commands to an Arduino. Finally, you will practice keeping A P I keys and credentials out of source code by loading them from environment variables and systemd or shell profiles on the Raspberry Pi. Each practiced objective is paired with a small verification step so you can confirm your device calls the A P I, stores the payload, and responds correctly. This setup prepares you for secure, testable IoT integrations.

HTTP provides a small set of standard methods that map naturally to IoT tasks. GET retrieves data: use it when a device or client needs to fetch configuration, the latest readings, or external data like weather. POST sends new data: use it when your device uploads a telemetry record or a log entry. PUT updates an existing resource, for example changing a device's saved configuration; it generally replaces or updates the target resource. DELETE removes a resource, such as unregistering a device or deleting old stored entries. A concrete example: a device posts a sensor reading with POST to the readings endpoint, a dashboard fetches recent readings with GET, an operator updates reporting settings with PUT, and a cleanup job deletes obsolete records with DELETE. A common misconception is thinking POST and PUT are identical. They are different in intent: POST creates or appends, while PUT is intended for an idempotent update. For IoT, that distinction matters when retries happen on poor networks — a repeated POST can create duplicate records while a properly designed PUT should not. As a takeaway, map your device operations to the right method, design endpoints to be safe on retry, and document expected behavior for clients.

The requests library is the go-to tool in Python for simple HTTP operations from devices. A GET request fetches a resource and returns a response object you can convert to JSON. For example, calling a public weather endpoint returns a JSON object where temperature typically sits under a main object and a temp key. You call response. json() to parse that payload into Python dictionaries and lists. A POST request sends data to a server. The chapter shows a POST that sends sensor fields using a payload dictionary to a Thingspeak-like update endpoint. Note the difference between sending form-encoded data with a data parameter and sending JSON with a json parameter; many APIs expect one or the other. A common error is printing or assuming keys exist in the JSON without checking; use methods that handle missing entries gracefully. Also never hardcode A P I keys—use environment variables and read them with os. environ. get. Practically, test both GET and POST from your device, watch response. status_code to confirm success, and print response text on failures to debug. Try the example GET for weather and the POST that uploads two fields to verify round-trip behavior before wiring these calls into your main device loop.

JSON is the most common payload format when calling web APIs. When your device receives JSON, it becomes a nested set of dictionaries and lists in Python after calling response. json(). The practical steps are: parse the JSON, check for expected keys, convert the extracted values to the needed type, and handle missing or malformed values. For example, the weather JSON usually nests main. temp under main, so access that path using safe access like dict. get and default fallbacks. Always validate the type — a numeric string may need conversion to float before storage. A concrete example: request weather, then obtain temperature with weather. get('main', {}). get('temp'). If the value is None, decide whether to retry or use a cached reading. A common misconception is trusting that the A P I always returns full data; networks and services fail, so include error handling and retry policies. Also consider that parsing large JSON structures on small devices uses memory; extract only relevant fields and avoid holding entire payloads when unnecessary. As a takeaway, treat JSON as structured data that must be validated and sanitized before being used by device logic or inserted into a database.

When consuming public APIs from an IoT device, follow a clear process that keeps reliability and security in mind. Step one: read the A P I documentation to learn required parameters and authentication. For example, many weather services require an A P I key and specific query parameters for city and units. Step two: implement a lightweight request using the requests library, check response. status_code, and parse response. json() to extract the fields you need. Step three: validate and transform values for your device logic, for instance converting a temperature to a float or mapping a string status to a numeric threshold. Step four: handle errors and network issues with retry logic, exponential backoff, and caching where appropriate so your device can continue operating if the external A P I is temporarily unreachable. Step five: secure A P I keys by storing them in environment variables and not in source control. A concrete example is fetching the current temperature and adjusting a fan speed based on a threshold. A common misconception is polling too frequently; public APIs often have rate limits. Design your device to poll only as often as necessary and cache results when possible. The result is a predictable, secure integration between device logic and external data sources.

REST APIs for IoT typically expose resources such as devices and readings through clear, resource-based URLs. The chapter lists common endpoints like GET /api/devices to list registered devices, GET /api/devices/001/readings to fetch recent readings, POST /api/devices/001/readings to upload a new reading, PUT /api/devices/001/config to update settings, and DELETE /api/devices/001 to remove a device. Two important architectural principles are stateless communication and clear resource modeling. Stateless means each request contains all information required to process it; the server does not rely on stored session state from previous calls. For IoT, stateless APIs simplify scaling, retries, and failure recovery. Resource-based URLs make intent explicit: an endpoint name indicates the object being manipulated. When designing such APIs, think about the data model for readings, how many results to return by default, and how to document expected payload shapes. A common misconception is coupling device transport state to the A P I; instead, design the A P I to accept well-formed JSON payloads and let the server handle persistence. As a takeaway, model devices and readings as resources, keep endpoints stateless, and document expected request and response formats for clients.
